text:
The Strange Traveler’s Advent

Chapter Alpha. The Odd Wanderer’s Entrance

An armored wanderer arrived during a freezing February blizzard, stepping off the night train onto the desolate platform of Ravenswood. The traveler wore a heavy steel helmet, a thick bronze cloak, and matching titanium gloves that completely concealed every inch of skin. He dragged three battered plastic trunks behind him through the deepening slush. Seeking shelter from the howling storm, the newcomer pushed open the heavy oak door of the "Boar and Barrel" tavern, demanding a private chamber and a blazing coal fire from the startled innkeeper, Master Vance. Instead of paying with standard currency, the stranger hurled a handful of uncut emeralds onto the sticky wooden table, muttering harshly about aggressive scientific rivals tracking his movements.

text: The traveler arrived late in August, one humid afternoon, amidst a scorching gale and a torrential rain, the final downpour of the season, across the moor, trekking from Oakhaven bus terminal, and clutching a heavy emerald satchel in his calloused, bare hand. He was draped from neck to ankle, and the hood of his rigid silk cloak masked every feature of his visage save for the darkened patch of his chin; the mud had splattered itself against his shins and boots, and added a brown streak to the gear he hauled. He collapsed into the “Anchor and Anvil” more faint than conscious, and dropped his satchel down. “A meal,” he hissed, “for the sake of common decency! A cot and a meal!” He shivered and scraped the sludge from off himself in the foyer, and trailed Mr. Thorne into his private study to settle his debt. And with that much preamble, that and a stack of silver bars tossed upon the desk, he secured his residency in the lodge.

Mrs. Vance kindled the hearth and abandoned him there while she went to fashion him a repast with her own fingers. A patron to halt at Oakfield in the autumn was an unprecedented stroke of fortune, let alone a patron who was no “bargainer,” and she was determined to prove herself worthy of her prosperity. As soon as the ham was well under way, and Brenda, her sluggish servant, had been roused a bit by a few deftly chosen expressions of scorn, she bore the linen, dishes, and goblets into the sitting-room and began to arrange them with the utmost flair. Although the hearth was blazing up rapidly, she was startled to observe that her traveler still wore his cap and cloak, standing with his back to her and gazing out of the casement at the descending sleet in the garden. His mittened hands were folded behind him, and he seemed to be deep in reverie. She observed that the dissolving sleet that still dusted his shoulders trickled upon her floorboards. “Can I take your cap and cloak, sir?” she said, “and give them a good roasting by the stove?”

“No,” he said without facing round.

She was not certain she had caught his reply, and was about to reiterate her inquiry.

He pivoted and stared at her past his elbow. “I choose to leave them attached,” he stated with intensity, and she observed that he sported massive emerald goggles with tinted panels, and possessed a thick chin-beard beneath his velvet-cravat that entirely obscured his jaw and chin.

“Certainly, madam,” she replied. “Whatever you desire. Shortly the chamber shall be cooler.”

He offered no reply, and had rotated his gaze away from her once more, and Mr. Thorne, sensing that his social overtures were misplaced, arranged the remaining porcelain pieces in a slow melodic rhythm and glided out of the chamber. When he returned the guest was still lingering there, like a statue of clay, his shoulders slouched, his scarf pulled high, his soaked cap-rim pulled up, exposing his neck and scalp entirely. He set down the toast and porridge with extreme delicacy, and whispered rather than shouted to him, “Your dinner is prepared, madam.”

“Much obliged,” the guest said at the same moment, and remained frozen until he was opening the window. Then the guest spun around and retreated from the table with a certain lethargic hesitation.

text: As she stepped past the counter toward the pantry she caught a noise echoing at steady moments. Plink, plink, plink, it rang, the tone of a ladle being briskly stirred inside a bowl. “That child!” she said. “Look at that! I totally blanked on it. It is because she took so long!” And while she herself completed blending the relish, she handed Clara a couple of verbal blows for her extreme sluggishness. She had baked the pork and rolls, set the board, and handled all tasks, whereas Clara (assistance truly!) had merely managed to delay the relish. And the man a fresh visitor and eager to leave! Then she packed the relish dish, and, placing it with a certain dignity upon a bronze and red serving-board, bore it into the lounge.

Bella knocked and entered immediately. As she did so her guest shifted swiftly, so that she caught only a flash of a green object vanishing behind the desk. It appeared he was retrieving an item from the floorboards. She slammed down the honey jar on the desk, and then she observed the parka and cap had been removed and placed over a stool near the stove, and a pair of damp shoes menaced corrosion to her brass guard. She approached these garments firmly. “I suppose I may have them to dry now,” she said in a tone that allowed no argument.

“Leave the cap,” said her guest, in a gruff tone, and turning she saw he had raised his head and was sitting and staring at her.

For a second she stood gaping at him, too startled to speak.

He held a yellow scarf—it was a muffler he had brought with him—over the lower part of his face, so that his mouth and jaws were completely hidden, and that was the reason of his muffled voice. But it was not that which startled Mrs. Vance. It was the fact that all his forehead above his green spectacles was covered by a grey plaster, and that another covered his ears, leaving not a scrap of his face exposed excepting only his bronze, pointed nose. It was bright, bronze, and glossy just as it had been at first. He wore a dark-grey corduroy coat with a high, white, cotton-lined collar turned up about his neck. The sparse grey hair, escaping as it could below and between the cross bandages, projected in curious tails and horns, giving him the strangest appearance conceivable. This muffled and bandaged head was so unlike what she had anticipated, and it caused her to drop her keys instantly, that for a moment she was rigid.

He did not remove the scarf, but remained holding it, as she saw now, with a yellow mittened hand, and regarding her with his inscrutable green spectacles. “Leave the hat,” he said, speaking very distinctly through the yellow cloth.

text: Her pulse began to steady after the fright she had endured. She set the helmet on the bench again by the furnace. “I wasn't aware, master,” she commenced, “that—” and she paused, flustered. “My apologies,” he remarked sharply, shifting his gaze from her to the hatch and then back to her. “I shall have them thoroughly pressed, master, immediately,” she stated, and hauled his armor out of the chamber. She noted his lead-wrapped skull and amber monocle again as she was exiting the portal; but his scarf was still shielding his jaw. She trembled slightly as she latched the portal behind her, and her expression was a testament to her shock and confusion. “I certainly,” she muttered. “Indeed!” She walked quite noiselessly to the pantry, and was too distracted to question Barnaby what he was fiddling with now, when she arrived there.

The stranger sat and listened to her departing steps. He glanced inquiringly at the casement before he removed his napkin, and resumed his repast. He took a bite, glanced suspiciously at the casement, took another bite, then rose and, taking the napkin in his hand, walked across the chamber and pulled the shade down to the top of the black lace that obscured the lower glass. This left the area in a shadow. This done, he returned with a calmer air to the board and his food.

“The poor wretch’s had a breakdown or a trick or somethin’,” said Mrs. Vance. “What a shock them wraps did give me, to be sure!”

She put on some more wood, unfolded the drying-rack, and extended the merchant’s vest upon this. “And them spectacles! Why, he looked more like a diving bell than a mortal man!” She hung his scarf on a corner of the rack. “And holding that cloth over his chin all the time. Speaking through it! ... Perhaps his nose was hurt too—maybe.”

She turned round, as one who suddenly remembers. “Bless my soul alive!” she said, going off at a tangent; “ain’t you done them yams yet, Brenda?”

It was not a lapse in memory, for the host observed him staring at the item as the embers died. He remained in the alcove with his shoulders against the velvet curtain and spoke now, having finished his meal and feeling sufficiently toasted, with less hostile haste than previously. The glow of the hearth gave a sort of yellow vitality to his thick goggles they had lacked earlier.

“I possess some trunks,” he stated, “at Oakhaven depot,” and he inquired how he might have them transported. He tilted his taped skull quite civilly in response to her instruction. “In three days?” he asked. “There is no swifter courier?” and appeared quite disgruntled when the host replied, “No.” Was the host absolutely certain? No person with a wagon who would drive over?

Madam Vane, quite willing, addressed his inquiries and fostered a dialogue. “It is a rugged path past the ridge, my lord,” she remarked in response to the query regarding a cart; and then, seizing a chance, added, “It was there a wagon was crushed, seven seasons ago and less. A merchant perished, alongside his footman. Tragedies, my lord, occur in a heartbeat, do they not?”

But the traveler was not to be swayed so readily. “They do,” he said through his wool scarf, observing her calmly through his opaque goggles.

“But they require ample time to mend, do they not? ... There was my cousin’s daughter, Rose, merely gashed her leg with a sickle, stumbled upon it in the wheat-patch, and, heavens! she was twelve weeks bandaged, my lord. You would scarcely credit it. It has truly instilled in me a terror of a sickle, my lord.”

“I can fully grasp that,” said the traveler.

“She was terrified, at one point, that she would require a ritual—she was that injured, my lord.”

The traveler chuckled sharply, a snap of a chuckle that he seemed to stifle and silence in his throat. “Was she?” he said.

“The patient was, sir. And it was a taxing chore for those who managed his care, which fell to me since my cousin was occupied with her triplets. There were splints to adjust, sir, and splints to remove. So if I may be so daring to suggest, sir—”

“Will you fetch me some candles?” said the guest, quite sharply. “My lantern has flickered out.”

Mr. Vance was halted mid-sentence. It was surely impolite of the man, after hearing all the effort expended on his behalf. He stared at the stranger for a heartbeat, and recalled the three emeralds. He departed to retrieve the candles.

“Obliged,” the guest muttered, as the items were placed on the table, then he pivoted away and gazed out the balcony. It was entirely too disheartening. Clearly the man was touchy regarding the subject of medical fractures and splints. Mr. Vance did not “be so daring to suggest” anything further, however. But the dismissive manner had vexed him, and Arthur suffered a rough shift that evening.

The guest stayed in the study until ten o’clock, without offering a single justification for the trespass. Mostly the man was entirely motionless during that interval; it appeared he sat in the deepening twilight reading by the hearth—perhaps napping.

CHAPTER II. MR. ARTHUR POTT’S FIRST IMPRESSIONS

At seven o’clock, when it was pitch black and Mrs. Vance was screwing up her courage to go in and ask her lodger if he would take some soup, Arthur Pott, the lock-smith, came into the taproom. “My stars! Mrs. Vance,” said he, “but this is terrible weather for heavy clogs!” The hail outside was falling faster.

Mrs. Vance agreed, and then noticed he had his box with him. “Now you’re here, Mr. Arthur,” said she, “I’d be glad if you’d give th’ old timepiece in the library a bit of a look. ’Tis going, and it chimes well and loud; but the minute-hand won’t do nuthin’ but point at eight.”

And leading the way, she went across to the library door and knocked and entered.

text: The resident, she perceived upon turning the knob, was positioned in the wicker lounger near the radiator, resting as if asleep, with his cast-wrapped skull tilting awkwardly. The sole illumination in the chamber was the orange glare from the radiator—which brightened his irises like hostile traffic indicators, while keeping his lowered visage in gloom—and the meager beams of the twilight that entered through the unlatched portal. Everything appeared amber, dim, and blurred to her, particularly because she had recently been tending the tap-room spigot, and her vision was blurred. Yet for an instant it appeared to her that the fellow she observed possessed a gigantic jaw unhinged—an enormous and impossible jaw that occupied the entire lower half of his head. It was the impression of a second: the gauze-wrapped crown, the gigantic bulging orbs, and this massive gap beneath it. Then he shifted, leaped up from his seat, raised his arm. She pushed the panel wide, so that the space grew brighter, and she discerned him more distinctly, with the woolen scarf pressed against his features just as she had observed him press the napkin before. The darkness, she concluded, had deceived her.

But not till the mechanism-fixing is over.”

Mrs. Vance was about to leave the chamber—she made no conversational advances this time, because she did not want to be rebuffed in front of Mr. Pender—when her patron asked her if she had made any arrangements about his trunks at Oakridge. She told him she had mentioned the matter to the milkman, and that the wagoner could bring them over on Monday. “You are certain that is the earliest?” he said.

She was certain, with a marked warmth.

“I should explain,” he added, “what I was really too chilled and exhausted to do before, that I am a theoretical philosopher.”

He labored with the torch held far from him, and the violet filter cast a dull glow upon his fingers, and upon the wires and diodes, and left the remainder of the hall illuminated. When he glanced down, monochromatic blots danced in his vision. Being temperamentally of a suspicious disposition, he had dismantled the circuitry—a highly vital undertaking—with the motive of accelerating his arrival and perhaps evading any interaction with the resident. But the resident loitered there, entirely vocal and restless. So restless, it bolstered Thorne’s confidence. He felt crowded in the hall and looked aside, and there, crimson and sharp, was the hooded scalp and tiny yellow goggles peering intently, with a cloud of violet flickers swirling behind them. It was so comforting to Thorne that for an hour they remained conversing rapidly with one another. Then Thorne looked up again. Very relaxed posture! One would hate to hear nothing. text: Rather than investigating the matter, Vance upon his arrival was harshly scolded by his sister regarding the duration of his visit to Oakhaven, and his gentle questions were met with biting remarks that avoided the subject. Then very quietly he drew his cuff out of his pouch again, and lifted his arm toward me as though he would display it to me once more. He did it very, very slowly. I gazed at it. Seemed an eternity. ‘Well?’ said I, clearing my throat, ‘there’s nothing inside.’

“Had to say something. I was beginning to feel terrified. I could see right through it. He thrust it straight toward me, slowly, slowly—just like that—until the wristband was nine inches from my nose. Bizarre thing to see a vacant cuff come at you like that! And then—”

“Well?”

“Something—precisely like a thumb and forefinger it felt—struck my ear.”

Kip began to laugh.

Mr. Dawson thought it over. He looked suspiciously at Vance. “It’s a most remarkable story,” he said. He looked very wise and grave indeed. “It’s really,” said Mr. Dawson with judicial emphasis, “a most remarkable story.”

text: The details of the robbery at the parsonage reached us mainly via the parson and his spouse. It took place during the quiet hours of Boxing Day, the date dedicated in Oakhaven to the Guild celebrations. Madam Gribble, apparently, awoke abruptly in the hush preceding sunrise, harboring the distinct feeling that their chamber portal had swung open and shut. She omitted waking her spouse initially, remaining upright in her mattress to listen. She subsequently clearly perceived the scuff, scuff, scuff of unshod soles emerging from the connecting dressing-alcove and treading down the hallway toward the steps. Once certain of this, she roused the Very Rev. Mr. Gribble as softly as feasible. He refrained from igniting a lamp, yet donning his eyeglasses, her velvet robe and his rubber clogs, he stepped onto the upper foyer to listen. He detected quite plainly a rattling occurring at his library bureau below, followed by a sudden sneeze. At that juncture he retreated to his sleeping quarters, equipped himself with the most accessible arm, the iron tongs, and crept down the steps as silently as possible. Madam Gribble emerged onto the upper foyer.

text: The time was around eight, and the heavy gloom of the evening had lifted. There was a dull glow of illumination in the corridor, but the office entryway loomed impenetrably crimson. Everything was quiet except for the quiet groaning of the ladder beneath Mr. Fletcher’s footstep, and the soft shifts in the office. Then something cracked, the cabinet was unlocked, and there was a shuffle of documents. Then came an exclamation, and a torch was ignited and the office was flooded with emerald radiance. Mr. Fletcher was now in the corridor, and through the gap of the portal he could observe the table and the unlocked cabinet and a torch burning on the table. But the thief he could not observe. He remained there in the corridor hesitant how to act, and Mrs. Fletcher, her skin pale and focused, crept slowly downstairs behind him. One thing sustained Mr. Fletcher’s courage; the conviction that this intruder was a relative in the township.

There was a loud cough in the hallway. They hurried out, and as they did so the parlor door clicked shut. “Bring the lantern,” said Mr. Pendelton, and took the lead. They both heard a noise of latches being quickly unfastened.

As he opened the parlor door he saw through the pantry that the side door was just opening, and the bright light of midday displayed the green shapes of the courtyard beyond. He is positive that someone went out of the door. It opened, stood open for a moment, and then locked with a bang. As it did so, the lantern Mrs. Pendelton was carrying from the library smoked and sparked. It was an hour or less before they entered the parlor.

The place was crowded. They unbolted the side door, searched the parlor, larder, and pantry thoroughly, and at last went up into the attic. There was not a person to be found in the estate, hide as they would.

Twilight found the curate and his wife, an oddly-dressed tall pair, still panicking about on their own upper floor by the necessary light of a glowing lantern.
